lines.text: It started as a heavy box in the boot of a car. This is how the mobile phone shrank, got smart, and ended up in almost every pocket on Earth.
Meet Martin Cooper, the Motorola engineer whose team built the first handheld mobile, and who made the first public call on one on a New York street in 1973.
Long before that, in 1946, AT&T launched the first mobile phone service, for phones built into cars, with only a handful of channels per city.
In 1979 the first cellular network opened in Tokyo, with the Nordic countries close behind. This was 1G: analogue, and voice only.
America got its own analogue network, AMPS, which split cities into cells that could reuse the same radio frequencies.
Then the first handheld phone anyone could buy: the Motorola DynaTAC. It weighed almost a kilo, cost nearly four thousand dollars, and earned a nickname, the brick.
Europe agreed on a digital standard, GSM. It brought roaming across borders, SIM cards and text messages, and became the most used mobile system in history.
With 2G, calls became digital data: harder to eavesdrop on, and with room for a little more.
That little more was the text message. Just a hundred and sixty characters, but it became how a generation talked.
In 1994 IBM sold a phone with a touchscreen, email and apps. The Simon is often called the first smartphone, though its battery lasted about an hour.
Two years later, Motorola's StarTAC flipped open, the first flip phone, small enough to clip to a belt.
Nokia went the other way: the Communicator opened like a tiny laptop, with a keyboard, email and even fax.
Symbian arrived to run phones like these. Nokia made it the leading phone software of the next decade.
In 1998 Iridium put phone service anywhere on Earth through satellites in low orbit. Its first owners went bankrupt, but the network lives on.
In Japan, Docomo's i-mode put email and websites on phones for millions, years ahead of the rest of the world.
The Nokia 3210 hid its aerial inside, let you swap its covers, and came with Snake. About a hundred and sixty million were sold.
Also from Japan, in 1999: emoji, little pictures for phone screens that now fill billions of messages a day.
WAP promised the web on your phone. In practice it was slow, cut-down pages, and most people gave up on it.
GPRS did better, adding always-on data to GSM, paid for by the amount you used. Email on the go was suddenly real.
In 2000 Sharp sold the first camera phone, in Japan. The way we take pictures was about to change.
The same year came the Nokia 3310, remembered as unbreakable, with a battery that lasted for days. Nokia sold well over a hundred million.
3G brought faster data: video calls, the mobile web, and the first apps. The road to the smartphone was open.
Picture messages followed. MMS let you send a camera phone photo to a friend, at a price.
The humble Nokia 1100, tough and cheap with a little torch, became the best-selling phone ever, and a first phone for many across Asia and Africa.
At the other end, the Motorola Razr was so thin and shiny it became a fashion item.
BlackBerry owners had BBM, fast, free messaging that showed when a message had been read, years before other apps.
In Kenya, M-Pesa let people send money by text from the simplest phone, giving millions a way to pay and save without a bank.
Nokia's N95 did everything: camera, GPS, Wi-Fi, music and the web. On paper, it was the best phone in the world.
Then, in 2007, Apple showed the iPhone: a full web browser and a multi-touch screen in your pocket. Nothing would be the same.
Its software, later named iOS, was built for touch, and when Apple opened it to outside apps, an entire economy was born.
For now, many still loved their keyboards. The BlackBerry Curve was the phone teenagers and office workers alike could not put down.
In 2008 the App Store opened, and anyone could sell software to millions of iPhone owners.
Google answered with Android, built on Linux and given to phone makers for free. It became the most used operating system in the world.
The first Android phone was the HTC Dream, with a screen that slid up to reveal a keyboard. Every Android since descends from it.
WhatsApp sent messages over the internet instead of paid texts. Today more than two billion people use it.
4G made it all fast: streaming video, maps and social media became everyday things on a phone.
Palm tried a fresh idea, webOS, with cards for apps and swipes between them. It failed on phones, but lived on in smart TVs.
In 2010 Samsung launched the Galaxy S, and became the iPhone's main rival.
Microsoft tried too, with bright tiles in Windows Phone, but it never found enough apps or users, and was given up.
In China, WeChat grew into an app for everything: messages, payments, shopping and more, for over a billion people.
Samsung's Galaxy Note came with a pen and a screen over five inches. People laughed at the size, and then everyone copied it.
The same year, Siri arrived on the iPhone 4S, putting a talking assistant in millions of pockets.
By 2014 your phone could be your wallet: with Apple Pay, you just held it to the card reader.
Not every launch went well. The Galaxy Note 7's batteries caught fire, and it was recalled worldwide and banned on planes.
In India, Jio launched with free calls and very cheap data, and brought hundreds of millions of people online.
The iPhone X dropped the home button for an edge-to-edge screen and face unlocking, and most phones followed its shape.
In 2019, 5G networks began rolling out, faster, quicker to respond, and ready for a world of connected devices.
And that same year, a phone that folds: the Galaxy Fold, the first widely sold phone with a bending screen.
From a brick in a car to a computer that folds in half, and the phone is still changing.
